title: Elevator Scope Gaps: Pit Access, Power Rough-In, and Commissioning Requirements
summary: Elevator pit access, power rough-in, and commissioning gaps cost GCs at buyout. Here's the scope language needed to close each one before bid day.
body_markdown:
**Elevator scope gaps don't show up during bid review. They show up at buyout — when the elevator sub hands back a list of exclusions the GC never saw coming.** Pit ladders, sump pumps, power rough-in, and commissioning assistance: each one is a line item someone has to own. If your scope language doesn't name the owner, the GC absorbs it.


This post breaks down the three most expensive elevator scope gap patterns on institutional and commercial builds: pit access requirements, power rough-in, and commissioning. For each one, you'll find the specific language that closes the gap before bid day.


## TL;DR


- Elevator scope gaps cluster in three areas: pit rough-in, power supply, and commissioning assistance.
- Most disputes trace back to "as per plans and specs" scope language — which tells the sub nothing about who owns what.
- Pit ladders, sump pumps, machine room conditions, and temporary power are the most commonly missed line items.
- Commissioning disputes are rising on institutional and healthcare projects because the elevator sub's AHJ inspection process pulls other trades back to site.
- The fix is specific document references and trade-tailored scope language written before the bid goes out.


## Why Elevator Scope Gaps Are Getting More Expensive


Elevator work sits at the intersection of at least four other trades: concrete, electrical, mechanical, and drywall. That overlap is where scope gaps breed. Every trade assumes someone else owns the interface work. Nobody does.


On institutional and healthcare builds, the problem compounds. Commissioning requirements from the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) are stricter. Inspection timelines are longer. And the cost of pulling other trades back to site for a failed inspection lands on the GC if the scope language doesn't say otherwise.


According to the Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Report, the average North American construction dispute was worth $60.1M in 2024. "Errors and omissions in contract documents" has consistently ranked as the leading dispute cause in North America. Elevator scope gaps are a textbook example of that category.


The[Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) documents specialty trade gaps in detail — including the $300K lead-lined glass omission absorbed by a GC under "readily inferable" language. Elevators follow the same pattern: the scope looks covered until it isn't.


## Gap #1: Pit Access Requirements


### What the elevator sub thinks they own


The elevator sub prices the car, the rails, the cab, and the drive system. They do not automatically price the civil and rough-in work that makes the pit usable. That includes:


- Pit access ladders (fixed steel, code-compliant)
- Pit lighting and outlets
- Sump pit and sump pump
- Pit drainage connection to building drain
- Waterproofing at pit walls (especially below grade)
- Pit door or hatch, including hardware and signage


Most of these items are in the drawings — spread across civil, architectural, and mechanical sheets. None of them are automatically in the elevator sub's price unless your scope language says so explicitly.


### The anti-pattern that creates the gap


The most common anti-pattern in elevator scope packages is "as per plans and specs." It's the single most-cited phrase in the[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) — and it's the most expensive one. It tells the sub to read documents that may contradict each other and leaves the ownership question unanswered.


A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it plainly: *"If you miss anything, they'll bill it."* That's not a criticism of subs — it's how the market works. Subcontractors have become faster at protecting their scope, and gentlemen's agreements don't hold the way they used to.


### Scope language that closes the pit gap


Your elevator scope package should name each pit item explicitly and assign it to a trade. Here's a working format:


- **Pit ladder:** "Furnish and install fixed steel pit access ladder per \[Drawing A-XXX, Detail X\]. Ladder to meet ASME A17.1 requirements. Coordinate with concrete for embedded anchorage."
- **Sump pump:** "Furnish and install sump pit and sump pump per \[Spec Section XX XX XX\]. Drain connection to \[civil/mechanical trade\]. Elevator sub to coordinate."
- **Pit lighting and receptacle:** "Permanent pit lighting and duplex receptacle per \[Electrical Drawing E-XXX\]. Included in electrical scope. Elevator sub to confirm requirements prior to rough-in."
- **Waterproofing:** "Pit wall waterproofing below grade included in \[concrete/specialty waterproofing scope\]. Elevator sub to verify conditions prior to equipment delivery."


The format is specific by design. As one Pre-Construction Lead described it — what they call the "peanut-butter test" — scope language needs to be as literal as a recipe: *"It's descriptive — bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar… You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"*


## Gap #2: Power Rough-In Requirements


### The three-way handoff problem


Elevator power rough-in involves at least three trades: the elevator sub, the electrical sub, and sometimes the mechanical sub (for machine room HVAC). The gap lives in the handoff between them.


The elevator sub submits power requirements after award — sometimes weeks after the electrical sub has already roughed in conduit. If the electrical scope doesn't account for the final elevator power schedule, the result is a change order. Usually more than one.


Common missed items in elevator power rough-in:


- Dedicated circuit to machine room or MRL (machine-room-less) drive cabinet
- Lighting panel in machine room
- Pit lighting circuit (separate from cab circuit)
- Telephone or emergency communication rough-in
- Conduit sleeves through rated floors and walls
- Temporary power for installation and testing


### Temporary power: the most contested line item


Temporary power for elevator installation and testing is the most consistently disputed item on elevator scope packages. The elevator sub assumes the GC provides it. The GC assumes it's included in the elevator price. The electrical sub has never heard of it.


This mirrors the generator field-conditioning disputes documented in the Scope Gap Playbook — where "millions in disputed costs" recurred across multiple projects because no scope language assigned the conditioning work to a specific trade. Temporary power for elevator installation follows the same logic: if the scope doesn't name it, nobody owns it.


Fix it with one line: *"Temporary power for elevator installation, testing, and commissioning to be provided by \[GC / electrical sub\]. Elevator sub to submit power requirements no later than \[X\] weeks after award."* That sentence closes the gap.


### Machine room conditions


If the project has a traditional machine room (not MRL), the room conditions need to be in scope before the elevator sub prices the job. Temperature, humidity, and ventilation requirements vary by drive type and manufacturer. If the mechanical scope doesn't account for them, the elevator sub will call it a changed condition at commissioning.


Add a coordination trigger to the scope: *"Machine room HVAC design to be coordinated with elevator sub shop drawings. Mechanical sub to confirm final design prior to \[milestone\]."*


## Gap #3: Commissioning Requirements


### Why commissioning disputes are rising


Elevator commissioning on institutional and healthcare projects now involves more stakeholders than it did five years ago. AHJ inspections, owner acceptance testing, and building system integration testing (for access control, fire recall, and BAS tie-ins) all pull other trades back to site.


The elevator sub prices the equipment and the installation. They don't automatically price:


- Assistance during AHJ inspection (waiting time, reinspection fees)
- Access control system integration (card readers, floor lockout)
- Fire alarm recall programming coordination
- BAS or building controls integration
- Owner acceptance testing support (beyond standard turnover)
- Cab interior protection during construction (and removal before inspection)


Each of these involves at least one other subcontractor. If the scope doesn't define who coordinates and who pays for extended attendance, the GC mediates — and usually absorbs.


### The "readily inferable" trap


Many GC contracts include language that makes the contractor responsible for work "reasonably inferable" from the contract documents. On elevator commissioning, owners and their legal teams use this language aggressively. Fire alarm recall is in the spec — therefore the elevator sub should have anticipated the integration work. Access control is in the drawings — therefore the coordination cost is inferable.


A Senior PM at a Canadian ICI GC described the shift: *"Our construction management clients expect us to find the scope gaps in the design too now. They expect us to be designers and engineers."* On elevator commissioning, that expectation is real. If the integration requirements are in the spec, even buried in Division 28 or a fire protection narrative, you own the coordination cost unless your scope language says otherwise.


### Scope language for commissioning


The most effective approach is to list commissioning activities explicitly in the elevator scope package and tag each one with a responsible party:


- **AHJ inspection assistance:** "Elevator sub to be on-site for initial AHJ inspection and one reinspection if required. Additional reinspections beyond one to be billed at \[rate\] per occurrence."
- **Fire alarm recall:** "Fire alarm contractor to program elevator recall sequence. Elevator sub to provide required interface documentation to fire alarm sub no later than \[milestone\]."
- **Access control integration:** "Low-voltage / access control sub to provide cab reader and controller. Elevator sub to provide rough-in requirements prior to cab installation."
- **BAS integration:** "BAS contractor to provide points list for elevator monitoring. Elevator sub to confirm available data points and communication protocol prior to \[milestone\]."
- **Owner acceptance testing:** "Elevator sub to provide \[X\] hours of on-site support during owner acceptance testing. Additional time billed at \[rate\]."


This is the habit described in the Scope Gap Playbook as "Clarifications, not just exclusions." Exclusion lists tell you what the sub won't do. Clarification lists assign ownership. You need both.


## The Document Problem Behind Every Elevator Gap


Most elevator scope gaps aren't caused by careless estimating. They're caused by fragmented documents. Pit requirements live in architectural drawings. Waterproofing is in the spec. Power requirements are in the electrical drawings. Machine room conditions are in a mechanical narrative. Commissioning requirements are in Division 14, Division 26, Division 28, and sometimes the owner's project requirements (OPR).


No estimator reads all of them in sequence, cross-referenced against each other, in the time available on a competitive bid. The gaps are structural — they're built into how construction documents are organized.

## Closing Elevator Scope Gaps Before Bid Day


The Eight Habits in the[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) apply directly to elevator scope packages. Three habits matter most here:


1. **Drawings-first, not boilerplate-first.** Start with the actual pit details, electrical one-lines, and commissioning specs — not last year's elevator scope template.
2. **Specific document references, not generic incorporation.** Cite the drawing number, the spec section, and the detail. "Per plans and specs" creates disputes. "Per Drawing A-201, Detail 3, and Spec Section 14 21 13" closes them.
3. **Front-load the buyout conversations.** If your elevator sub has questions about who owns pit drainage or AHJ reinspection costs, you want those questions answered before award — not at commissioning six months later.


A Senior PM at a Toronto mid-market developer framed the standard clearly: *"If we could catch three scope gaps or three missed items on every scope of work, then this thing pays for itself."* On elevator alone, three items — pit ladder, temporary power, and commissioning assistance — are worth catching every single time.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are the most common elevator scope gaps on commercial GC projects?


The three most common are pit access items (ladder, sump pump, lighting), power rough-in (dedicated circuits, temporary power for installation), and commissioning support (AHJ inspection attendance, fire alarm recall coordination, BAS integration). Each involves a handoff between trades that scope language often doesn't resolve.


### Who is responsible for the elevator pit ladder and sump pump?


It depends on your scope language — which is the problem. Neither item is automatically in the elevator sub's price. Pit ladders typically fall to concrete or rough carpentry. Sump pumps often fall to mechanical or plumbing. Your scope package needs to name the responsible trade explicitly, with a drawing reference.


### How should GCs handle temporary power for elevator installation?


Assign it in writing before the bid. Specify which trade provides it, what the power requirements are, and by what date the elevator sub must submit their power schedule after award. Leaving this item unassigned is one of the most consistent elevator change order triggers.


### Why are elevator commissioning disputes increasing on institutional projects?


AHJ inspections on healthcare and institutional projects are more complex — fire recall integration, access control tie-ins, and BAS connections pull multiple trades back to site. Elevator subs price installation, not extended commissioning coordination. If your scope doesn't define attendance limits and reinspection costs, the GC absorbs the overrun.


### What scope language should a GC use for elevator fire alarm recall coordination?


Assign the programming responsibility to the fire alarm contractor and require the elevator sub to provide interface documentation by a specific milestone. Don't leave it as a coordination item without an owner. "Coordinate with fire alarm sub" is not a scope assignment — it's a gap.


### How does "readily inferable" contract language affect elevator scope?


If commissioning requirements are anywhere in the project documents — even buried in Division 28 — the owner may argue that coordination costs were inferable and therefore the GC's responsibility. The best defense is scope language that explicitly assigns each commissioning activity to a named trade before the contract is signed.
